name: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate

lead: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is a stabilised, water-soluble form of vitamin C used as a cosmetic antioxidant.
Most published work covers formulation and stability; human trials of its looks effects are few.

paras: It functions primarily as an antioxidant in cosmetic formulations, per the Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment.
A cosmetic safety assessment covers SAP alongside other vitamin C compounds; no specific harms were found in the sources reviewed.

lead: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate (SAP) is a water-soluble, phosphate-ester derivative of vitamin C used in cosmetics, mainly as an antioxidant. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review's safety assessment of ascorbic acid and its salts and esters, including SAP, describes them as functioning primarily as antioxidants in cosmetic formulations [1].

SAP is promoted as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid. Laboratory studies have examined its stability in microemulsions and in formulations containing lipoic acid and vitamins A and E [2][3]. Human evidence includes a registered trial of a 5% SAP lotion for acne and trials of topical antioxidant regimens for photoaging [4][5].

paras: Vitamin C is described as labile, with oxidation accelerated by light, oxygen, heat and higher pH [6]. Derivatives such as SAP are used partly to address this. Studies have investigated SAP in microemulsions [2], liposomes for cutaneous photoprotection [7], and hyaluronic acid microspheres for dermal delivery [8].
The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel's final safety assessment covered SAP together with ascorbic acid and several salts for use in cosmetics [1].

A comparison of vitamin C derivatives in topical formulations containing lipoic acid, vitamin A and vitamin E examined their stability [3]. Related work on ascorbyl palmitate in microemulsions studied stability of that derivative [9].

SAP has also been used in non-cosmetic experiments, including a hydrogel with stem cells for wound healing in mice and diabetic rats [10][11] and in studies of restoring bond strength after tooth bleaching [12].

A completed trial registered as NCT00714454 tested a 5% sodium L-ascorbyl-2-phosphate lotion for acne vulgaris; results are not summarised in the sources reviewed [4]. A registered trial (NCT04835259, status unknown, n=90) examined topical antioxidants for photoaging [5], and a 300-person phase 3 trial studied an antioxidant dentifrice for gingivitis [13]. Published outcomes for cosmetic brightening or anti-ageing with SAP alone were not located.
